## Prerequisites
Assumes [The method](overview.qmd) (the loop) and [The model](model.qmd) (how a plant is
parameterized). This page uses Fisher information and the Cramér–Rao bound throughout — see
the [glossary](glossary.qmd) for CRB, dispersion, and D-optimal if they are new.
:::

## From model to measurement budget

Every measurement experiment faces the same tension: a finite amount of
drive power (bounded by actuator saturation) and a finite measurement time (bounded
by how long an interferometer can be held in a non-standard state).  The question
is not how much to drive, but where.

The Fisher information matrix `I(θ)` is the bridge.
It quantifies, for a given model θ and experimental design (Pxx, T, Pyy),
how many nats of information the experiment carries about each parameter
and each pair of parameters.  Its inverse is the Cramér–Rao lower bound — the best
any unbiased estimator can do.

For a single-input / single-output LTI system `G(f; θ)` driven with PSD `Pxx(f)`,
measured in additive noise with PSD `Pyy(f)`, over time `T`:

$$
I_{ij}(\theta) = 2\,T \int_0^{f_s/2}
  \frac{P_{xx}(f)}{P_{yy}(f)}
  \operatorname{Re}\!\left[
    \frac{\partial G^*(f;\theta)}{\partial \theta_i}
    \frac{\partial G(f;\theta)}{\partial \theta_j}
  \right] df
$$

(the factor 2 is the circular-complex measurement-noise convention also carried by
the maximum-likelihood fit). `system_ident` exposes this as `fisher.fisher_matrix`
and `fisher.parameter_covariance`; the leading denominator coefficient is held
fixed at 1 (the standard transfer-function gauge), so its row and column are
removed and the matrix is full-rank for any well-excited measurement.

## The dispersion function

Let $M(f)$ be the marginal Fisher information per unit drive power at
frequency $f$ — the per-Hz integrand of $I(\theta)$ with the $P_{xx}(f)$ factor
stripped out:

$$
M(f) = \frac{2\,T}{P_{yy}(f)}
  \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\frac{\partial G^*}{\partial \theta}\,
  \frac{\partial G}{\partial \theta}\right],
\qquad
I(\theta) = \int P_{xx}(f)\, M(f)\, df .
$$

The dispersion function (Pintelon & Schoukens §5.4.2) is the scalar

$$
\nu(f) = P_{\text{tot}} \,\operatorname{tr}\!\left[\, I(\theta)^{-1}\, M(f)\,\right] ,
$$

the sensitivity of the information ellipsoid to a marginal unit of drive power
placed at $f$. High $\nu(f)$ marks the bins where the resonance is strongly
excited and the readout noise is not overwhelming the response, which is where
each extra Hz of drive returns the most parameter information.

By construction the power-weighted average of $\nu$ is the parameter count,
$\int P_{xx}(f)\,\nu(f)\,df / P_{\text{tot}} = \operatorname{tr}[I^{-1}I] = n_\theta$.
The equivalence theorem of D-optimal design (Kiefer–Wolfowitz) then says the
information-maximising spectrum is the one for which $\nu(f) = n_\theta$ on the
support of $P_{xx}$ and $\nu(f) \le n_\theta$ elsewhere. Reweighting drive power
toward high-$\nu$ bins under a fixed total-power budget is the Pintelon–Schoukens
fixed-point iteration that flattens $\nu$ to this optimum.

## Interactive comparison

The figure below shows the result for a simple 1 Hz resonance with Q = 20.
The top panel is the plant |G(f)|, annotated at the resonance peak.
The bottom panel compares the drive ASDs: the optimal allocation
(gold, filled) against a flat sweep of equal total power (gray, dashed).
Hovering over either curve reads exact values; zooming in on the resonance shows
how tightly the optimal drive brackets it.

```{python}
#| label: fig-optimal-excitation
#| fig-cap: "Optimal excitation vs flat drive of equal power, for a 1 Hz / Q=20 resonance. The optimal drive concentrates power at the resonance; the flat drive spreads it uniformly. Zoom in on 0.8–1.2 Hz to compare."
#| code-summary: "Optimal vs flat excitation"
import sys, pathlib
_p = pathlib.Path.cwd()
for _c in [_p, *_p.parents]:
    for _d in (_c, _c / "docs"):
        if (_d / "sysid_plots.py").exists() and str(_d) not in sys.path:
            sys.path.insert(0, str(_d))
import numpy as np
import sysid_plots as sp

from system_ident.model import TFModel
from system_ident.design.pintelon import optimal_excitation
from system_ident.fisher import parameter_covariance, dispersion

freq   = np.linspace(0.1, 4.0, 600)
model  = TFModel.from_resonances([(1.0, 20.0)], gain=1.0)
Pyy    = np.ones_like(freq)
Px_tot = 1.0

Pxx_opt  = optimal_excitation(freq, model, Pyy, Px_tot, n_iter=6)
Pxx_flat = np.full_like(freq, Px_tot / (freq[-1] - freq[0]))

T_tot    = 256.0
cov_opt  = parameter_covariance(freq, model, Pxx_opt,  Pyy, T_tot)
cov_flat = parameter_covariance(freq, model, Pxx_flat, Pyy, T_tot)
ratio    = np.max(np.diag(cov_flat)) / np.max(np.diag(cov_opt))

sp.excitation_design(
    freq, np.abs(model.eval(freq)), np.sqrt(Pxx_opt), np.sqrt(Pxx_flat),
    ratio=ratio, annotations=[(1.0, "f₀ = 1 Hz, Q = 20")]).show()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Reading the figure

The optimal drive is not centred exactly at f₀ — it is shaped by both the
Jacobian ∂G/∂θ (which peaks near f₀ but is nonzero over a bandwidth set by 1/Q)
and the readout noise PSD Pyy(f).  With flat white noise the result is nearly
Lorentzian, but on real hardware where Pyy rises steeply below ~0.3 Hz,
the optimal drive shifts to higher frequencies where the SNR is better.
:::

## The dispersion function, flattened

The D-optimal fixed point is reached when the dispersion $\nu(f)$ equals the
parameter count $n_\theta$ across the support of the drive. Below, the flat drive
leaves $\nu$ sharply peaked at the resonance, meaning available information is not
collected, while the optimal drive has flattened $\nu$ to $n_\theta$ there, which is
the signature of convergence.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dispersion
#| fig-cap: "Dispersion ν(f) for the flat vs optimal drive. The optimal drive flattens ν to the parameter count nθ across the resonance support (Kiefer–Wolfowitz equivalence); the flat drive leaves it peaked."
#| code-summary: "Dispersion ν(f): flat vs optimal"
import plotly.graph_objects as go

nu_flat, gamma_flat = dispersion(freq, model, Pxx_flat, Pyy)
nu_opt,  gamma_opt  = dispersion(freq, model, Pxx_opt,  Pyy)
n_theta = gamma_opt.shape[0]

fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=freq, y=nu_flat, mode="lines",
              line=dict(color=sp.GRAY, width=2.0, dash="dash"), name="ν(f) — flat drive"))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=freq, y=nu_opt, mode="lines", fill="tozeroy",
              fillcolor="rgba(200,151,58,0.12)", line=dict(color=sp.GOLD, width=2.6),
              name="ν(f) — optimal drive"))
fig.add_hline(y=n_theta, line_dash="dot", line_color="rgba(31,138,192,0.6)",
              annotation_text=f"  nθ = {n_theta}", annotation_position="right",
              annotation_font=dict(size=sp.SZ_ANNOT, color=sp.SKY, family=sp.FONT))
fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Frequency  [Hz]")
fig.update_yaxes(title_text="dispersion ν(f)")
sp.style(fig, height=360).show()
```

## The information ellipse

"Maximise $\log\det I(\theta)$" has a geometric reading. The Cramér–Rao covariance
$\mathrm{Cov}(\hat\theta) = I(\theta)^{-1}$ defines a confidence ellipse in parameter
space, centred on the truth; its area is $\propto \sqrt{\det\mathrm{Cov}} =
1/\sqrt{\det I}$. D-optimal design therefore shrinks the ellipse. Below, the joint
$(f_0, Q)$ region for the same 1 Hz / Q = 20 resonance under the flat drive (gray) and the
Fisher-optimal drive (gold), both of equal total power. The flat drive puts almost no power
at the resonance, so it barely constrains $Q$ and its ellipse extends far up the $Q$ axis;
the optimal drive concentrates there and collapses the region. The covariance is computed in
physical $(f_0, Q)$ coordinates — gain marginalised out — from the same Fisher integral, so
the axes are the reported parameters.

```{python}
#| label: fig-info-ellipse
#| fig-cap: "The 1σ (f₀, Q) confidence ellipse for a flat drive (gray) vs the Fisher-optimal drive (gold) of equal power. D-optimal design minimises the ellipse area (det Cov); it also rotates the ellipse, trading f₀ against Q information where the resonance is most informative. The flat drive barely constrains Q, so its region extends well beyond the plotted optimal."
#| code-summary: "The (f₀, Q) confidence ellipse, flat vs optimal"
from scipy.integrate import trapezoid

f0_t, Q_t, g_t = 1.0, 20.0, 1.0                       # the truth (ellipse centre)

def _fq_cov(Pxx):
    """Marginal (f0, Q) covariance from the (f0, Q, gain) Fisher, at drive Pxx."""
    base = (f0_t, Q_t, g_t)
    step = [1e-6 * f0_t, 1e-6 * Q_t, 1e-6 * g_t]
    H = lambda a, b, c: TFModel.from_resonances([(a, b)], gain=c).eval(freq)
    d = []
    for i in range(3):
        hi, lo = list(base), list(base)
        hi[i] += step[i]; lo[i] -= step[i]
        d.append((H(*hi) - H(*lo)) / (2 * step[i]))
    w = Pxx / Pyy
    I = 2 * T_tot * np.array([[trapezoid((d[i].conj() * d[j]).real * w, freq)
                               for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)])
    return np.linalg.inv(I)[:2, :2]                   # (f0, Q) block, gain marginalised

cov_flat_fq = _fq_cov(Pxx_flat)
cov_opt_fq = _fq_cov(Pxx_opt)
area_ratio = np.sqrt(np.linalg.det(cov_flat_fq) / np.linalg.det(cov_opt_fq))

sp.info_ellipse(
    [dict(mean=(f0_t, Q_t), cov=cov_flat_fq, label="flat drive",
          color=sp.GRAY, width=2.4, dash="dash"),
     dict(mean=(f0_t, Q_t), cov=cov_opt_fq, label="optimal drive",
          color=sp.GOLD, width=3.0)],
    title=f"1σ (f₀, Q) confidence ellipse — the optimal drive reduces its area "
          f"{area_ratio:.0f}× (D-optimal minimises det Cov)").show()
```

The fixed-point iteration reaches this optimum in a few passes (the same 3–5 iterations that
flatten $\nu$ above); the result is the smaller region in the figure title — the
$\sqrt{\det\mathrm{Cov}}$ the D-optimal criterion is defined to minimise.

## Variance reduction in numbers

```{python}
#| label: tbl-variance
#| echo: false
print(f"{'Excitation':<28} {'Max parameter variance':>24}   {'Relative'}")
print("-" * 65)
print(f"{'Flat (equal power)':<28} {np.max(np.diag(cov_flat)):>24.3e}   1.0 ×")
print(f"{'Optimal (Fisher-matched)':<28} {np.max(np.diag(cov_opt)):>24.3e}   {1/ratio:.4f} ×  ({ratio:.0f}× lower)")
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## How the iteration converges

`optimal_excitation(freq, model, Pyy, Px_tot, n_iter=3)` runs three rounds of the
fixed-point update.  In practice 3–6 iterations are enough; convergence can be
verified by comparing the output ASD across successive calls.
The API is:

```python
from system_ident.design.pintelon import optimal_excitation

Pxx = optimal_excitation(
    freq,       # frequency array [Hz]
    model,      # TFModel (current prior)
    Pyy,        # readout noise PSD [units²/Hz]
    Px_tot,     # total drive power budget [units²]
    n_iter=3,   # fixed-point iterations
)
```
:::

## What happens at each iteration

Starting from a flat initial guess `Pxx⁽⁰⁾`, each iteration applies the
multiplicative dispersion reweighting of `design.pintelon.optimal_excitation`:

1. Build the Fisher matrix `I(θ; Pxx⁽ᵏ⁾)` and the per-bin information density
   `M(f)` from the current model's Jacobian and the readout noise `Pyy`.
2. Evaluate the dispersion `ν⁽ᵏ⁾(f) = P_tot · tr[I⁻¹ M(f)]` at every bin.
3. Reweight and renormalise:
   `Pxx⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾(f) ∝ Pxx⁽ᵏ⁾(f) · ν⁽ᵏ⁾(f)`, rescaled so `∫ Pxx⁽ᵏ⁺¹⁾ df = Px_tot`.
   Power flows toward bins with `ν > n_θ` and away from bins with `ν < n_θ`; the
   fixed point is reached when `ν` is flat (`= n_θ`) across the support.
4. Repeat. Two or three iterations usually suffice — pushing further makes the
   design lean too heavily on the (still imperfect) prior model.

After convergence the excitation is synthesised as a periodic multisine via
`excitation.multisine_from_psd`: lines placed on the synchronous bin grid at
amplitudes `√(2·Pxx·df)`, with low-crest Schroeder phases and a leading Tukey
ramp. Because the waveform is periodic over the analysis window, the response DFT
is leakage-free — see [the method overview](overview.qmd) and the
[worked examples](../examples/01-single-resonance.qmd).

## Resolvability of two modes {#when-are-two-modes-resolvable}

A non-parametric habit holds that two resonances closer than one linewidth
`Γ = f₀/Q` (or one DFT bin `1/T`) are unresolvable — merged under a single peak.
That is a statement about peak-picking, not about information. A parametric
maximum-likelihood fit does not read peaks; it fits the whole complex FRF, and the
Fisher information about the mode separation `Δf` is finite for any `Δf > 0`.
The question is therefore not whether a doublet is resolvable but at what
measurement budget, and the CRB answers that with a number.

Take two resonances of equal linewidth `Γ` separated by `Δf`, and treat the pair as
resolved when the CRB on the separation drops below the separation itself,
`σ(Δf) < Δf` (the modes are more than 1σ apart). Because the Fisher information is
linear in the budget `∝ SNR·N`, `σ(Δf)² ∝ 1/(SNR·N)`, so the budget needed to reach
`σ(Δf) = Δf` is a pure function of `Δf/Γ`. It is computed here directly from the
two-mode Jacobian — the same `2T·Pₓₓ/P_yy · Re[∂G*∂G]` Fisher used above:

```{python}
#| label: fig-resolvability
#| fig-cap: "The CRB-computed resolvability boundary for a parametric two-mode fit. Below one linewidth (Δf/Γ < 1) — where non-parametric peak-picking gives up — the required budget rises as a steep but finite power of Γ/Δf. Sub-linewidth resolution is a cost, not a wall. The SRM within-plane 1.512/1.527 Hz pair (Q≈50) is marked."
#| code-summary: "CRB on the mode separation vs Δf/Γ"
from IPython.display import display, Markdown

def _two_mode_frf(f, f1, f2, Q):                       # two unit-residue resonances
    d1 = 1 - (f / f1) ** 2 + 1j * (f / f1) / Q
    d2 = 1 - (f / f2) ** 2 + 1j * (f / f2) / Q
    return 1.0 / d1 + 1.0 / d2

def _sigma_sep(f0, Q, dsep, *, span=30.0, npts=8000):   # σ(Δf) at unit budget
    Gam = f0 / Q                                        # linewidth
    f1, f2 = f0 - dsep / 2, f0 + dsep / 2
    fg = np.linspace(f0 - span * Gam, f0 + span * Gam, npts)
    h = 1e-6 * f0
    dG1 = (_two_mode_frf(fg, f1 + h, f2, Q) - _two_mode_frf(fg, f1 - h, f2, Q)) / (2 * h)
    dG2 = (_two_mode_frf(fg, f1, f2 + h, Q) - _two_mode_frf(fg, f1, f2 - h, Q)) / (2 * h)
    I = np.array([[np.sum((a.conj() * b).real) for b in (dG1, dG2)] for a in (dG1, dG2)])
    C = np.linalg.inv(I)
    return np.sqrt(C[0, 0] + C[1, 1] - 2 * C[0, 1])     # σ of (f2 − f1)

f0_r, Q_r = 1.52, 50.0                                  # SRM {T,R,Y} within-plane pair scale
Gam_r = f0_r / Q_r
ratio = np.unique(np.r_[np.logspace(np.log10(0.15), np.log10(5.0), 40), 1.0])
# budget to reach σ(Δf)=Δf is (σ_unit/Δf)^2; normalise to the one-linewidth case
budget = np.array([(_sigma_sep(f0_r, Q_r, r * Gam_r) / (r * Gam_r)) ** 2 for r in ratio])
ref = budget[np.argmin(np.abs(ratio - 1.0))]           # the one-linewidth budget
budget = budget / ref
expo = np.polyfit(np.log(ratio[ratio <= 1.0]), np.log(budget[ratio <= 1.0]), 1)[0]

dsep_wp = 0.015                                         # 1.512 ↔ 1.527 Hz
r_wp = dsep_wp / Gam_r
b_wp = (_sigma_sep(f0_r, Q_r, dsep_wp) / dsep_wp) ** 2 / ref

sp.resolvability_map(
    ratio, budget, rayleigh=1.0,
    points=[(f"1.51 Hz pair  ({r_wp:.2f} Γ)", r_wp, b_wp)]).show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
display(Markdown(
    f"The computed boundary follows **budget ∝ (Γ/Δf)<sup>{-expo:.1f}</sup>** below one "
    f"linewidth — a steep power law, close to (and slightly gentler than) the pure-tone "
    f"**SNR·N ≳ (Γ/Δf)⁴** rule of thumb. The SRM within-plane 1.512/1.527 Hz pair sits at "
    f"**Δf/Γ ≈ {r_wp:.2f}** (sub-linewidth): resolving it by frequency alone costs **≈ "
    f"{b_wp:.0f}×** the budget of a one-linewidth pair — a finite record-length / SNR price, "
    f"not a physical wall. (In the plant it is cheaper to sidestep: the 0.67 Hz doublet "
    f"is spatial and resolves at no extra budget by "
    f"[plane decoupling](../examples/10-srm-hsts.qmd), while the 1.51 pair shares one plane "
    f"and is the genuine frequency-super-resolution case.)"))
```

This is the feasibility gate in one figure: "resolution-limited" is a budget
statement, not a boundary. A one-linewidth / one-bin / Rayleigh limit should never be
quoted against a parametric fit — compute `σ(Δf)` from the CRB, and if a doublet is
genuinely sub-linewidth, report the SNR·N (record length or drive) that would resolve it.

## References

Pintelon & Schoukens, *System Identification: A Frequency Domain Approach*,
2nd ed., Wiley-IEEE Press, 2012 — §5.4.2 (dispersion-function optimal input
design), within the book's Fisher-information / Cramér–Rao framework. The
D-optimal equivalence theorem is due to Kiefer & Wolfowitz (1960).

[LIGO-G2101503](https://dcc.ligo.org/LIGO-G2101503) — Fisher-information
expressions for suspension parameters, the form ported into `fisher.fisher_matrix`.
